hero.title: Protecting community cats in Orihuela Costa.
hero.lead: We're a team of volunteers who feed, neuter and look after the cat colonies along the Orihuela coast, every day. Fewer litters, healthier cats and calmer streets.
hero.earTitle: A cat with a clipped ear tip?
hero.earText: It means the cat is neutered, vet-checked and part of a cared-for colony.

work.title: Much more than leaving food out
work.lead: Every colony has volunteers who know each cat individually. This is what we do:

items.title: Feeding and cleaning
items.text: Food and water at set places and times. We always clean up afterwards.

items.title: Neutering
items.text: We trap humanely, take each cat to the vet and return it to its colony.

items.title: Health checks
items.text: We keep a census of every colony and act quickly on injuries, illness and new arrivals.

items.title: Good neighbours
items.text: We talk with residents and communities, and work with Orihuela Town Council to get colonies officially recognised.

steps.title: TNR in three steps
steps.lead: It's the method Spain's animal welfare law (Law 7/2023) sets out for managing cat colonies.

items.title: Trap
items.text: With safe, humane traps and as little stress as possible.

items.title: Neuter
items.text: A vet neuters and checks the cat, and clips one ear tip so it can be identified.

items.title: Return
items.text: It goes back to its colony, where we keep caring for it for life.

steps.link: More about TNR and the law

benefits.title: A cared-for colony is good for the whole neighbourhood
benefits.lead: Well managed, community cats give back more than you'd think.

items.title: Fewer rodents
items.text: They keep rats and mice away, without poison.

items.title: Quiet nights
items.text: No heat means no yowling, fighting or spraying.

items.title: No new litters
items.text: Neutered cats don't breed, and they hold their territory.

items.title: Public health
items.text: Vet-checked cats and clean feeding spots.

items.title: Lower costs
items.text: Neutering once costs less than removing litters every year.

items.title: Community
items.text: Caring together brings neighbours closer and teaches children respect.

law.title: Since 2023, the law protects them
law.text: Law 7/2023 recognises community cats and requires town councils to manage cat colonies using TNR. It's no longer a matter of goodwill: it's a legal duty.

meaning: Colonies need feeding every day of the year, including August and Christmas. That only works if many of us share the load.
You're also the face of the association for local residents: you explain what we do and why a cared-for colony makes the neighbourhood better.

faq.q: Do I have to live in Orihuela Costa?
faq.a: For colony shifts it helps to live nearby. If not, you can help with donations, sharing our posts or one-off campaigns.

faq.q: How much time do I need?
faq.a: A feeding shift takes 30 to 60 minutes. Consistency matters more than hours: if you commit to one day a week, the cats count on it.

faq.q: Can I help if I'm under 18?
faq.a: Yes, with an adult and your family's permission. Information stands are a good place to start.

faq.q: I already feed some cats on my own. What should I do?
faq.a: Get in touch. We'll help you get the colony neutered, registered and fed in line with local rules. That way both the cats and you are protected.

faq.q: What if I find a kitten or an injured cat?
faq.a: Message us on WhatsApp with a photo and the area. If it's in immediate danger, take it to an emergency vet. If they're healthy-looking kittens, don't move them: their mother may be nearby.

tnr.metaDescription: What TNR is, why it works and what Spain's Law 7/2023 says about community cats.
tnr.title: The TNR method
tnr.lead: Trap, neuter, return: the humane, effective way to manage cat colonies, and the one the law requires.

what.title: What TNR is
what.text: TNR stands for trap, neuter, return (CER in Spanish). Every cat in a colony is neutered and returned to its territory, where volunteers feed them and keep an eye on their health. The colony stops growing and, over time, gets smaller naturally.

steps.title: Trap
steps.text: Humane traps, set at feeding time and watched at all times.

steps.title: Neuter
steps.text: At the clinic the cat is neutered, dewormed and checked. Under anaesthetic, one ear tip is clipped: the international sign of a neutered cat.

steps.title: Return
steps.text: Once recovered, it goes back to the exact spot where it was trapped. Its colony is its home.

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.text: Volunteers keep feeding the colony, log every cat and neuter any newcomers.

why.title: Why it works
why.lead: Removing cats has never solved the problem. TNR does:

items.title: It stops breeding
items.text: A female cat can have two or three litters a year. Without neutering, a small colony grows fast.

items.title: It prevents the vacuum effect
items.text: Remove a colony and unneutered cats move in to take its place. A stable, neutered colony stops that.

items.title: It reduces nuisance
items.text: No heat, no yowling, fighting or spraying: the main reasons residents complain.

items.title: Healthier cats
items.text: They fight less, roam less and get regular vet checks.

items.title: It's humane and lawful
items.text: No healthy animals are killed, and it's the method set out in Law 7/2023.

items.myth: If you feed them, more cats will come.
items.fact: Breeding makes colonies grow, not food. Feeding at set times is what lets us trap and neuter every cat.

items.myth: Best to take them somewhere else.
items.fact: The vacuum effect means other cats would arrive. And the law favours managing colonies where they are, not removing them.
Cats in a managed colony are vet-checked and dewormed. With basic hygiene, the risk is very low.

items.myth: They'd be better off in a home.
items.fact: Most aren't used to people and would suffer indoors. Kittens and friendly cats are put up for adoption.

law.title: What the law says
law.lead: Spain's Law 7/2023 of 28 March on the protection of animal rights and welfare, in force since 29 September 2023, has a chapter on cat colonies.

items.title: It recognises community cats
items.text: A community cat lives freely but is tied to a territory. A colony is a group of these cats that, being poorly socialised, can't easily be handled but lives close to people.

items.title: It sets TNR as the method
items.text: Trap, neuter and return by non-harmful means, as part of comprehensive, non-lethal colony management.

items.title: It involves town councils
items.text: They must run colony management programmes covering census, neutering and health control, with the involvement of animal protection groups.

items.title: It requires pet cats to be neutered
items.text: So that fewer cats end up on the street, with the exceptions the law allows.

items.title: It punishes cruelty
items.text: Abandonment and cruelty are banned. Since the 2023 reform of the Criminal Code, animal cruelty can carry a prison sentence.

law.regional: In the Valencian Community, Regional Law 2/2023 of 13 March on the protection, welfare and keeping of companion animals also applies. Each town council sets out in its bylaws how colonies are registered and managed.
law.disclaimer: General information only: this is not legal advice.
law.boe: Read Law 7/2023 in the BOE (in Spanish)

rights.title: Their rights today
rights.lead: Under current law, a colony cat has the right to:
items: Be treated with dignity, free from cruelty, poisoning or abandonment
Be fed and cared for by those who manage its colony
Receive vet care and be neutered as part of a TNR programme
Not be put down, except for euthanasia prescribed by a vet to end its suffering
rights.reportText: Call 112 or 062 (Guardia Civil, SEPRONA), or the Local Police. If it's safe, take photos or video and note the time and place. Then message us: we'll help you report it.

items.title: Rodent control
items.text: They keep rats and mice away from homes and gardens, with no poisons that put pets and children at risk.

items.title: Peaceful coexistence
items.text: A neutered colony doesn't yowl in heat, fight or spray.

items.title: Public health
items.text: Vet supervision and clean feeding spots, which unmanaged cats don't have.

items.title: Savings
items.text: TNR solves the problem in the long run, so it costs less than repeated removals.

items.title: Education
items.text: Colonies teach children and young people to respect animals and shared spaces.

items.title: Neighbourliness
items.text: Each colony builds a network of neighbours who help each other and look after their area.

contact.privacyText: This site has no forms and stores none of your data. If you message us, we'll only use your details to reply.

p: In accordance with article 10 of Spanish Law 34/2002 on information society services and e-commerce (LSSI-CE), this notice identifies the owner of this website, whose purpose is to present the association's work, explain the TNR method and make it easy to get in touch and collaborate.
Access to this website is free and requires no registration. Visitors agree to make appropriate use of its content, in accordance with the law and good faith.
The texts, illustrations and logos on this website belong to the association or are used with permission. You may share them for non-commercial awareness purposes, citing the source.

This website links to third-party services such as Teaming for donations, WhatsApp for contact, and Spain's Official State Gazette. The association is not responsible for their content or privacy policies, which we recommend you read.
This legal notice is governed by Spanish law.

This website has no forms, doesn't let you create accounts, uses no tracking cookies or analytics tools, and stores no personal data about visitors. This policy explains what happens to your data only if you choose to contact us or collaborate.
{name}, Tax ID (CIF) {cif}. You can contact us at {email}.

Like any web server, the hosting provider may technically and temporarily log IP addresses and request data to keep the service secure and working. The association doesn't use these logs to identify you or build profiles.
Fonts are served from our own server, so your browser doesn't connect to third-party services when loading the site.

sections.h: If you email us or message us on WhatsApp
p: We'll process the data you give us (name, phone number or email and the content of your message) solely to reply to you and, if you want to volunteer, to coordinate your involvement. The legal basis is your consent when contacting us and, for volunteering, managing the relationship established with you.
We'll keep your data for as long as needed to handle your enquiry or while you collaborate with the association, and then delete it. We don't share it with third parties unless legally required.

WhatsApp is a service provided by WhatsApp Ireland Limited, which processes your data as an independent controller under its own privacy policy; this may involve international transfers covered by the mechanisms provided for in the GDPR.
Donations are made on the Teaming platform, which is responsible for any data you provide there under its own privacy policy. This website never receives or stores payment details.

You can exercise your rights of access, rectification, erasure, objection, restriction of processing and portability by writing to {email}. If you believe we haven't handled your rights properly, you can lodge a complaint with the Spanish Data Protection Agency (www.aepd.es).
If you're under 14, please ask your parent or guardian to contact us on your behalf.

We don't use any cookies (no analytics, advertising or social media cookies), and we don't load third-party content that sets them. Your language is part of the page address (/es or /en), so we don't need a cookie to remember it either. That's why you won't see a cookie banner.
If you click a link to Teaming or WhatsApp, you'll leave this website, and those services may use their own cookies under their policies.
You can view and delete cookies in your browser settings at any time.
